messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
messages.body_plain:
spOccupancy cannot fit the Rota-type multispecies occupancy model. It fits a community occupancy model without species interactions. That said, if that is what you need, it is a great package. As far as I know it is also somewhat limited in the random effects structure it supports.

If you need complex random effects, your best choice is probably to code the model yourself in JAGS/Nimble or Stan.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
messages.body_plain:
Just to add to Ken's response. I would say it's not only possible to include species-specific variables in the first order models, but critical to getting meaningful inference from these models into co-occurrence of species. If you have unmodeled heterogeneity in occupancy, this is soaked up by the interaction terms, and so can be problematic if a missing covariate impacts both species (for example, if both species respond positively to covariate x, and you do not include it in the first order models, and you fit a constant interaction on f12, this will result a positive interaction term being estimated erroneously). Good to be cognizant of this in any interpretation of these models.

Species-specific covariates on the interaction terms would seem less obviously justified (but it really depends on what the hypotheses you are testing is). I don't understand what you mean by "to explore the interaction between area and connectivity on occupancy" but fitting habitat covariates on interaction terms models heterogeneity in co-occurrence as a function of that covariate (distinct from the species' individual responses to that covariate, which you fit in the first order models).

 It is also worth considering the sample size requirements of these models - these models require a lot of data to support them (even for simple constant interaction terms, recent preprint by Cowans et al. suggest >400 sites when co-occurrence is strong), fitting covariates on interaction terms is very costly in terms of sampling requirements,

Josh

messages.subject: Accounting for low detection with occuMulti
messages.subject_clean: Accounting for low detection with occuMulti
messages.body_plain:
Hello again, everyone!

I’m using the occuMulti function to assess single-season occupancy and co-occurrence of four rodent species across the Bay Area. My data are structured as a list of imputed datasets with four rows for each of 76 sites (one per species), columns for each site- and/or species-specific independent variable (e.g., Area, Dist_urban, Above_MHW, Connectivity, Effort, and Year), and columns for detection/non-detection data for each species across sampling events.

When fitting the null model, the detection probabilities for each species are quite low (0.38, 0.27, 0.38, and 0.09). From my understanding of MSOMs, low detection values can cause issues, such as poor occupancy and species interaction estimates. I attempted to incorporate detection-level covariates (Effort and Year), but this didn’t yield better results, with the top model ~Effort + Year producing weighted detection probabilities of 0.24, 0.28, 0.81, and 0.11, respectively.

I also tried restructuring the detection/non-detection data for a removal model, but this didn’t work due to mismatched numbers of missing observations across species. Unfortunately, I can’t return to the field and do not have additional detection-level covariates to assess.

Does anyone have suggestions for how to proceed with low detection probabilities or approaches I might have missed?

Thanks in advance!
Thanks,
Kristin

> Just to add to Ken's response. I would say it's not only possible to include species-specific variables in the first order models, but critical to getting meaningful inference from these models into co-occurrence of species. If you have unmodeled heterogeneity in occupancy, this is soaked up by the interaction terms, and so can be problematic if a missing covariate impacts both species (for example, if both species respond positively to covariate x, and you do not include it in the first order models, and you fit a constant interaction on f12, this will result a positive interaction term being estimated erroneously). messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am an Asst. Prof in Fisheries , Wildlife, and Conservation Sciences at Oregon State University and have funding and am currently recruiting two graduate students, 1 masters and 1 PhD (https://fwcs.oregonstate.edu/).

Corvallis / Oregon is beautiful, there are mountains, forest, and ocean, a dream place for any ecologist.

Both projects will be hierachical modeling and model development focused (hense posting here, but also with lots of fieldwork live-trapping and camera trapping small mammals, and their predators) so if you like the idea of the combination of being outdoors but also doing cool quantitative work with an applied focus please check these out.

The masters project is focused on developing non-invasive monitoring methods and models for small mammal populations (https://jobs.rwfm.tamu.edu/view-job/?id=102411). This project will involve comparing SCR applied to intensive live-trapping data with enclosed camera traps and drones mounted with thermal cameras with model development for both the latter two.

The PhD project is on how interactions between predators, parasites, and the environment influence the population dynamics of a cyclical endemic vole (https://jobs.rwfm.tamu.edu/view-job/?id=102410) and will be focused on building integrated population demographic models to test hypotheses (predation, disease, competition, weather, season) about drivers of interannual cycles of gray-tailed voles (an endemic vole here in the Willamette Valley). This will involve data collection (live trapping, camera trapping, biologging etc.) and and model development.

See links for full job posting and requirements. Positions start in Fall 2025. We will we reviewing applications after Feburary 15th and applications recieved before then will get priority.

Feel free to contact me (joshua....@oregonstate.edu) with any questions,

All the best

Josh

messages.subject: Dynamic multispecies occupancy with interactions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

I am asking this question here because I hope it may be of general interest to some.

We have occupancy data for two bird species with very directed interactions; one is a predator of the other. It's multi-year and we may or may not distinguish more than one kind of occupied site (such as the typical 'occupied without repro' and 'occupied with repro').

My favourite approach would be to have a multistate, dynamic occupancy model with a Waddle-type of species interaction, where we use the presence/absence of the predator as a predictor in the model for the prey. We can and eventually probably will fit such a model in JAGS, but as a learning journey for the student, would like to fit as much as possible also in unmarked. What are our options ?
We will likely explore the data with colext() for single-species, single-state dynamic occupancy models.
Then, we can use function occuMS() to fit single-species, multistate dynamic occupancy models
But what about species interactions ? Here, we 'only' have the Rota et al models, with function occuMulti(), which does not support data from multiple years, right ?
And then, what about the Waddle-et al type of species interactions ? I think I heard rumours that a beta version for fitting this model might be just around the corner ?
Thanks for advice and sorry in case I overlooked something important because I didn't do my homework.

Best regards   ---- Marc

Hi Marc,

At the moment, yes, the only type of interaction model supported is the Rota model via occuMulti.

I have working beta code for the single-season Waddle model. The model fitting works, I just never finished implementing all the necessary methods and tests and then got distracted with other projects. I can upload this to a branch on Github in the meantime if there's interest so you and others can try it.

I will also note that Mike's 'wiqid' package supports the very similar Richmond version of the model (I believe also single-season only).

It is very likely I will eventually finish the Waddle model and get it into the released version of unmarked (probably not in the super-near future). It is less likely, but possible, I'd add support for the dynamic version of the model (it's probably more likely I'd add support for random effects and thus stacked models).

I think it's pretty unlikely I'd add support for a dynamic, multi-state version. I think that's too specific of a model structure to justify all the development/maintenenance that would be required. Of course if there are others out there that want to work on implementing this in unmarked I'd welcome that!

Ken

Dear Friends and Colleagues (and apologies for cross-posting),

We are very pleased to announce that we are taking applications for the 25-26 intake of our MSc in Statistical Ecology (see attached).

The MSc aims to give students:
a sound understanding of the statistical foundations of modern methods in statistical ecology
the knowledge and skills to use these methods effectively
experience of applying them to real-world problems, under the supervision of experts, some of whom are leading researchers in this field

The Programme involves two semesters of taught courses and a 3-month summer research dissertation. It is taught by staff at the interdisciplinary Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/). The summer dissertation includes optional placements with collaborators in the UK or abroad, to give students experience of dealing with real-world problems in statistical ecology.

More information is available here: https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/subjects/statistics/statistical-ecology-msc/

Hi Kristin,

There are other ways you could use for assessing overdispersion in the context of MSOMs using the 'occuMulti' function. For instance, you could use the Deviance-Based Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) Test. It basically relies on a parametric bootstrap that can be used to simulate new datasets under the fitted model, and compare observed deviance with the simulated distribution. If the observed deviance is much higher than the simulated values, overdispersion is likely.

Anyway, with regards to the Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test, overdispersion is a serious problem if the variance inflation factor ĉ is much higher than 1.5. In your case, the value is very close to 1.5. So, I don't think it represents a serious problem. If the model performs well (e.g., no strong residual patterns), you might not need major adjustments.

Hope this will help!

Best,
Marcello

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristin,

In this case you don't have to plot a residual vs fitted diagnostic. As you correctly said, it would be uninformative. By implementing the Deviance-Based Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) Test you should obtain a chart like the attached one.

Meaning of the graph:
Distribution of simulated deviances: The bars of the histogram show how the deviances derived from the simulations are distributed. Each simulation generates a deviance, which represents how well the simulated data fit a model similar to the one you fitted to your real data. Essentially, these deviances simulate how well a model might fit the data in hypothetical scenarios, considering various random variables.
Observed deviance (dashed red line): The dashed red line represents the observed deviance, which is calculated from your model using the real data you collected. It serves as the "benchmark" against which the simulations are compared. If the observed deviance aligns with the distribution of simulated deviances (i.e., it falls within the range of the histogram), it indicates that the model fits the real data well. If the observed deviance is much higher or lower than the simulated distribution (i.e., falling outside the range of the histogram), it might suggest that the model doesn't fit the real data well.
In this example, the dashed red line falls within the range defined by the histogram. This means that the model fits the real data well (as confirmed by the non-significant p-value obtained).

Another method for residual diagnostic would be using the Moran's I Test for Spatial Autocorrelation implemented in the 'spdep' R package. However, as I reported in the previous e-mail, your variance inflation factor value is just slightly outside the threshold value (i.e., 1.5) used to indicate severe overfitting. Therefore, I think you should not have problems with parameter estimates.

Best,
Marcello

Hi,

Just to clarify the information on the plot attached by Marcello from
mb.gof.test( ) which computes the MacKenzie and Bailey GOF test (but
not yet for multispecies models):
-the function simulates data based on the fitted model and computes the
chi-square statistic for each iteration;
-the chi-square is comparing the frequencies of each detection history
vs the frequencies predicted by the model;
-the goodness-of-fit test on binary data using a chi square requires
pooling. In mb.gof.test( ), observations are pooled for each detection
history yielding the frequencies, but other forms of pooling can also
be considered (across visits or sites), see examples in Kéry and Royle
AHM vol 1.

Hope it helps,

Marc
